claims.text: The proposed starting material is a nearly equiatomic five-component transition-metal alloy.
The starting nanoparticles have a BCC crystal structure.
Randomly distributed elements with different atomic radii produce severe local lattice distortion.
Annealing at 500–900°C for 100–1000 hours can induce atomic diffusion, phase separation, or grain growth.
A VEC near 4.7 promotes elastic isotropy in BCC refractory high-entropy alloys.
Thermal stability is governed by a kinetic bottleneck in which lattice distortion impedes diffusion more strongly than the thermodynamic driving force promotes precipitation.
Severe lattice distortion creates a high energy barrier for atomic migration and causes sluggish atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for precipitation.
The combination of high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion prevents nucleation and growth of secondary phases.
The proposed stability mechanism requires bulk diffusion to be the rate-limiting step.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles introduces surface-diffusion pathways that bypass barriers associated with bulk lattice distortion.
Below a critical diameter of 5 nm, surface energy and surface-mediated diffusion overwhelm the sluggish-diffusion mechanism.
Nanoparticles larger than 5 nm remain single-phase BCC with minimal grain growth and no precipitation after elevated-temperature annealing.
Nanoparticles smaller than 5 nm undergo rapid coarsening or phase separation.
The nanoparticles exhibit elastic isotropy similar to bulk counterparts.
Traditional alloy phase-stability models primarily use thermodynamic equilibrium calculations such as CALPHAD.
Conventional alloys generally show rapid precipitation and grain growth at 500–900°C and lack kinetic hindrance from severe lattice distortion.
Significant deviation from VEC 4.7 causes elastic anisotropy and may produce lattice instability.
Specific binary interactions can drive rapid spinodal decomposition that is not mitigated by configurational entropy.
HEA behavior can follow conventional thermodynamic stability rules rather than being controlled by high entropy or sluggish diffusion.

contradictions.description: The material is repeatedly described as a five-component alloy, but the concrete example NbTaTiV contains only four named elements.

Rapid coarsening or phase separation below 5 nm is the hypothesis's predicted boundary behavior, yet the falsification rule says that observing this same behavior would falsify the hypothesis. That result would confirm the stated size-dependent prediction rather than refute it.
